content: 1. Personal protective equipment (PPE) must meet the needs of healthcare workers (HCWs) in terms of fit, comfort, mobility, and ease of donning and doffing. Among participants surveyed, 31% identified comfort as the most significant challenge when wearing PPE, followed by issues with sizing and fit (27%), donning and doffing (14%), mobility (12%), material durability (12%), and other factors such as ease of use and PPE weight (3%). This highlights the critical role of donning and doffing features in the overall acceptance of PPE by HCWs. 2. A simulation study conducted by Poller et al. (2018) in the United Kingdom identified a unified PPE ensemble for clinical responses to high-consequence infectious diseases. This ensemble provided full protection against contamination during the simulation. It included a wide, extra-long, medium-thickness plastic apron, similar to those used in endoscopy. However, a higher fit to protect the upper chest was desired, as no such apron existed. A simple modification, such as tearing the neck loop in the middle to tie both the neck and waist areas, was deemed acceptable and significantly improved protection. 3. Kilinc-Balci et al. (2015) tested 22 commercially available single-use isolation gowns for barrier and strength properties using ASTM International standards (D5034, D5733, D1683, F1671), WHO guidelines for Ebola and Marburg diseases, and AAMI PB70 liquid barrier classification standards. Results showed significant variability in the barrier and strength properties of existing isolation gowns. Nine of the 22 gowns (41%) failed to meet the AAMI PB70 requirements for liquid barrier performance at the level specified by the manufacturer. These findings support the use of aprons for additional protection. 4. No studies were found that evaluated the environmental impact of single-use disposable PPE, exposures during cleaning and disinfection of aprons, breaches in cleaning and disinfection practices, or the transmission of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) or Marburg Virus Disease related to PPE breaches or ease of doffing. 5. Regarding head and neck protection, no studies provided direct evidence on the transmission or incidence of EVD or Marburg Virus Disease related to PPE use for head and neck skin protection. Two simulation studies addressed heat stress outcomes for HCWs wearing additional head/neck covering PPE (hoods). These studies found very low-certainty evidence that such PPE increased physiological and subjective measures of heat exhaustion compared to PPE without head/neck covering. Additionally, low-certainty evidence suggested that head/neck covering PPE resulted in less contamination but more human errors during donning and doffing compared to PPE without such coverage. 6. Zamora et al. (2006) conducted a prospective, randomized, controlled crossover study comparing two PPE ensembles. The enhanced respiratory and contact precautions (E-RCP) ensemble included a head covering (without neck skin coverage), goggles, and a face shield. The powered air-purifying respirator (PAPR) system used had outer and inner protective layers. The anterior neck, forearms, wrists, and hands were identified as the most likely zones for contamination. 7. Suen et al. (2018) conducted an experimental study with 59 participants who performed PPE donning and doffing. Fluorescent solution was applied to the PPE surface to estimate contamination levels. Three PPE ensembles were tested: PPE 1: Neck-to-ankle outfit, N95 respirator, hood, disposable face shield, surgical gown, boots, and double gloves. PPE 2: Head-to-ankle coverall, N95 respirator, hood, disposable face shield, boots, and double gloves. PPE 3: Neck-to-ankle outfit, N95 respirator, no hood, disposable face shield, isolation gown, shoes, and single latex gloves. Results showed that PPE 1 was less contaminated in regions protected by the hood (hair, head, and neck) compared to PPE 3, supporting the use of head and neck skin coverage. 8. Coca et al. (2015) conducted a simulation study using a thermal manikin to assess the time to reach a critical core temperature of 39°C while wearing four different PPE ensembles under two ambient conditions (32°C/92% humidity and 26°C/80% humidity). Results suggested that encapsulation of the head and neck region increased heat sensation. Another study by Coca et al. involved participants walking on a treadmill for 60 minutes while wearing different PPE ensembles. Subjective perceptions of heat and exertion were significantly higher for ensembles with additional head/neck coverage. 9. Den Boon et al. (2014) surveyed 44 frontline physicians and nurses deployed to West Africa during the 2014–2016 EVD outbreak. Heat and dehydration were reported as major issues by 64% of respondents using a hood. Despite this, 93% perceived the hood as posing low or extremely low safety risks, and 60% reported no or minor impairment in their ability to provide patient care. 10. Grélot et al. (2016) assessed thermal strain in 25 HCWs during the 2014 EVD outbreak. PPE use, in accordance with WHO regulations, resulted in moderate but safe thermal strain after approximately one hour of wear. 11. Sprecher et al. (2015) reported on a meeting convened by Médecins Sans Frontières in 2014 to address PPE concerns. Participants included representatives from the CDC, WHO, NIH, and PPE manufacturers. Polyethylene fabric hoods that fully covered the head and neck were favored over surgical head coverings. The meeting emphasized the need for better evidence in PPE selection. 12. Overall, evidence on the effectiveness of head/neck covering PPE in reducing contamination and improving safety is of low to very low certainty. While such PPE may reduce contamination, it may also increase heat stress and human errors during donning and doffing. Further research is needed to optimize PPE design and usage.
